questions.prompt: A button is covered by an overlay. Why can a normal Playwright click wait rather than immediately act?

choices.text: A matching selector alone proves the element is actionable.
The button must be able to receive pointer events.
All clicks wait for every network request on the page to finish.
The locator automatically removes overlays before clicking.

questions.explanation: Click actionability includes receiving events. A selector match is insufficient, and auto-waiting does not remove application overlays.

sources.title: Playwright auto-waiting
sources.claim: Playwright checks actionability such as visibility, stability, receiving events and enabled state before clicking, then fails on timeout.

questions.prompt: An assertion checks isVisible once immediately after an async update and flakes. Which approach fits Playwright guidance?

choices.text: Use an awaited toBeVisible web-first assertion.
Add a permanent ten-second sleep before every assertion.
Ignore visibility failures when CI is under load.
Check the locator object’s truthiness instead of the DOM.

questions.explanation: Web-first assertions retry until the condition or timeout. Immediate checks race, while fixed sleeps and ignored failures weaken tests.

sources.title: Playwright best practices
sources.claim: Playwright recommends user-facing locators and web-first assertions that retry instead of manual immediate state checks.

questions.prompt: A test fails on its first run and passes on its first retry. How does Playwright classify it?

choices.text: Passed with no evidence of instability.
Failed even though a retry succeeded.
Skipped because retries never execute failed tests.
Flaky.

questions.explanation: Retry success after initial failure is flaky. It is distinct from first-run success and from exhausting all retries.

sources.title: Playwright test retries
sources.claim: Playwright labels first-run success passed, retry success flaky, and exhaustion of retries failed; retries do not remove the underlying failure.

questions.prompt: A CI-only test failure needs inspection of actions and page state. Which artifact is most directly useful?

choices.text: A screenshot alone, assuming it records every prior network and action step.
A trace started after the failed worker exits, assuming it recovers prior actions.
A Playwright trace captured on the first retry.
Only the final exit code with every other artifact deleted.

questions.explanation: A recorded trace captures actions and page state during execution. A screenshot or exit code does not reconstruct the sequence, and starting tracing after failure cannot recover earlier events.

sources.title: Playwright best practices
sources.claim: Playwright recommends traces on first retry to investigate CI failures and warns against tracing every test due to overhead.

questions.prompt: A button stays disabled for the entire action timeout. What should a normal click do?

choices.text: Automatically submit its form without delivering a click.
Fail with a timeout rather than silently bypass enabled state.
Enable the button in the application and then click it.
Report success because the selector matched exactly one button.

questions.explanation: Normal actions respect actionability. Playwright does not repair disabled application state or report successful interaction from a selector match alone.

sources.title: Playwright auto-waiting
sources.claim: Click actionability checks can fail with a timeout when the target remains disabled.

questions.prompt: A loading label should disappear after a request. Which approach avoids a fixed sleep?

choices.text: Await a web-first assertion that the label is hidden.
Sleep once and assume every machine has the same latency.
Read the label text before triggering the request.
Treat the existence of a locator as evidence of disappearance.

questions.explanation: An awaited condition-based assertion handles the expected change. Fixed timing and locator existence do not verify the final DOM state.

sources.title: Playwright best practices
sources.claim: Web-first assertions retry the condition instead of checking an immediate snapshot.

questions.prompt: Which normal-click checks can Playwright perform? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Wait for the target to be stable and enabled.
A visible but disabled button passes all normal-click actionability checks.
Treat a DOM match as proof that all actionability checks passed.
Remove every obstructing application element automatically.
Wait for the target to be visible.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Movement and disabled state affect actionability. B is incorrect: Normal click checks enabled state as well as visibility. C is incorrect: Matching and actionability are different. D is incorrect: Playwright waits rather than repairing the application. E is correct: A click requires a visible target.

sources.title: Playwright auto-waiting
sources.claim: Playwright checks actionability such as visibility, stability, receiving events and enabled state before clicking, then fails on timeout.

questions.prompt: Which choices improve end-to-end test resilience? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Prefer long CSS chains that depend on every wrapper element.
Use fixed sleeps as the primary proof of readiness.
Test user-visible behavior rather than private component internals.
Use locators based on roles and accessible names.
Await web-first assertions for asynchronously changing state.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Structural selectors are brittle under markup changes. B is incorrect: A delay does not verify a condition. C is correct: Behavior-focused tests reflect the intended contract. D is correct: User-facing attributes are less tied to DOM implementation. E is correct: Retrying assertions handle expected timing variation.

sources.title: Playwright best practices
sources.claim: Playwright recommends user-facing locators and web-first assertions that retry instead of manual immediate state checks.

questions.prompt: Which retry statements match Playwright behavior? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A successful retry proves there is no test or application issue.
Retries require every test to share state with the preceding test.
A test passing on its first attempt is classified as passed.
A test passing only after a retry is classified as flaky.
A passing retry changes the initial failure into first-attempt passed status.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Retry success does not explain the original instability. B is incorrect: Isolated tests can be retried independently. C is correct: No retry was needed. D is correct: The initial failure remains visible. E is incorrect: Playwright distinguishes retry success as flaky rather than first-attempt passed.

sources.title: Playwright test retries
sources.claim: Playwright labels first-run success passed, retry success flaky, and exhaustion of retries failed; retries do not remove the underlying failure.

questions.prompt: Which practices support diagnosing CI browser failures? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Keep tests isolated so a retry can reproduce its own setup.
Capture a trace on the first retry for failure investigation.
Inspect trace actions and state rather than guessing from timing alone.
Trace every test as the recommended default regardless of overhead.
Discard all failure evidence whenever a retry passes.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Independent state simplifies failure reproduction. B is correct: It supplies evidence for an intermittent failure. C is correct: Recorded evidence helps locate the failing interaction. D is incorrect: The guide recommends first-retry tracing rather than always-on traces. E is incorrect: Flakiness still needs investigation.

sources.title: Playwright best practices
sources.claim: Playwright recommends traces on first retry to investigate CI failures and warns against tracing every test due to overhead.
